concept.centerRule: Concept → character anchors → events, promises, signs, words, blood, places, actions, consequences, tensions, and later memory. Character anchors keep covenant attached to real biblical relationships rather than letting it become an abstract theological category.

characterAnchors.label: God
characterAnchors.note: Initiates, remembers, establishes, renews, judges covenant breach, promises restoration, and is repeatedly described as covenant keeper.

characterAnchors.label: Noah
characterAnchors.note: The first explicit covenant language in the biblical sequence gathers around Noah, his descendants, living creatures, flood memory, and the rainbow sign.

characterAnchors.label: Abraham
characterAnchors.note: Promise, offspring, land, covenant-making, name, circumcision, oath, and later covenant memory gather around Abraham.

characterAnchors.label: Israel
characterAnchors.note: At Sinai and beyond, covenant becomes public national relationship, words, signs, obedience, breach, remembrance, exile, renewal, and prophetic hope.

characterAnchors.label: Moses
characterAnchors.note: Moses mediates covenant words, blood, tablets, intercession, renewal, and later becomes a remembered covenant figure in Paul and Hebrews.

characterAnchors.label: David
characterAnchors.note: House, offspring, sonship, throne, and forever promise are later explicitly remembered as covenant with David.

characterAnchors.label: Jeremiah
characterAnchors.note: Jeremiah publicly names covenant breach and gives the canonical new-covenant promise later quoted in Hebrews.

characterAnchors.label: Ezekiel
characterAnchors.note: Ezekiel joins covenant language to remembered betrayal, peace, reunification, Davidic shepherding, and sanctuary presence.

characterAnchors.label: Jesus
characterAnchors.note: Jesus speaks covenant language over the Passover cup; later texts call him mediator of a new covenant and connect covenant with his blood.

characterAnchors.label: Paul
characterAnchors.note: Paul revisits Abraham, Sinai, promise, sign, meal memory, covenants of promise, Moses’ veil, and new-covenant ministry in several letters.

concept.throughline: Covenant moves through Scripture as announced promise, established relationship, sign, oath, public words, blood, peoplehood, land, priesthood, kingship, remembered obligation, broken relationship, renewal, prophetic hope, meal language, mediation, and later scriptural argument. The recurring concept stays connected while its participants, forms, and literary work change.

edges.basis: Hold the two signs together without treating “sign” as if it always works the same way. Both passages call something a covenant sign, but one is placed in the clouds for all flesh while the other is commanded in the flesh of Abraham’s male household.
edges.label: Two covenant signs

edges.basis: Read each scene on its own terms before noticing what covenant-making looks like in different narrative settings. Both scenes enact covenant with bodies and spoken words, but Abram receives the promise in darkness while Israel answers through a public, mediated ceremony.
edges.label: Covenant made / covenant ratified

edges.basis: Compare signs by frequency, participants, and action rather than assuming identical function. Both signs are said to endure, but the rainbow is seen in the clouds while Sabbath is repeatedly practiced by Israel.
edges.label: Sign once seen / sign repeatedly practiced

edges.basis: Keep the breach visible while reading the renewal. Israel’s breach and the covenant renewal belong to one sequence, yet the renewal does not erase the broken tablets, judgment, or Moses’ intercession.
edges.label: Calf / renewed covenant

edges.basis: Notice how later covenant renewal reuses public reading, response, and witnesses in new circumstances. Both assemblies publicly bind themselves to covenant words, but their leaders, witnesses, records, and historical pressures differ.
edges.label: Shechem / Josiah

edges.basis: Let Psalm 89 show how later Scripture names and expands the narrative promise. Psalm 89 remembers the Davidic covenant with language from the house promise while relocating it into praise and later lament.
edges.label: Promise / remembered covenant

edges.basis: Read the lament as part of the same psalm, not as a problem to solve outside it. The same psalm declares an enduring covenant and then describes the crown cast down, leaving promise and apparent collapse together.
edges.label: Promise / apparent collapse

edges.basis: Notice explicit reuse: Isaiah itself tells the reader to remember Noah. Isaiah explicitly recalls Noah while speaking a covenant of peace, but the prophetic address changes the audience, setting, and announced form of security.
edges.label: Noah / covenant of peace

edges.basis: Allow the quotation to remain visible so the reader can distinguish Jeremiah’s wording from Hebrews’ framing. Hebrews quotes Jeremiah’s new-covenant promise while framing it within an argument about a better ministry and the aging of the first covenant.
edges.label: Promise / quotation

edges.basis: Stay within Ezekiel and watch recurring covenant language accumulate. Both Ezekiel passages promise covenant peace, but one centers a Davidic shepherd and secure dwelling while the other joins everlasting covenant, sanctuary, and divine presence.
edges.label: Peace / everlasting peace

edges.basis: Hold the shared blood/covenant vocabulary together without erasing the distinct scenes. Both scenes join covenant words to blood, but Sinai applies sacrificial blood to altar and people while Jesus identifies the cup with his own approaching death.
edges.label: Blood of covenant / new covenant cup

edges.basis: Compare event and memory rather than treating the later practice as another Last Supper narrative. Paul transmits the meal tradition he received, yet his repetition addresses a divided assembly and emphasizes remembrance and proclamation until the Lord comes.
edges.label: Meal / remembered meal

edges.basis: Keep Genesis chronology visible while reading Paul’s argument about it. Genesis commands circumcision as covenant sign while Romans argues from the order of faith and sign, pressing the same sequence into a different claim about ancestry.
edges.label: Sign / sequence reread

edges.basis: Read the Exodus scene first so the later use does not replace it. Paul reuses Moses’ shining face and veil while contrasting fading glory with the ministry he identifies with the Spirit.
edges.label: Shining face / covenant ministry

edges.basis: Keep the quoted/recalled Sinai details distinct from Hebrews’ claims about Christ. Hebrews recalls first-covenant blood while extending the comparison into death, inheritance, cleansing, and heavenly ministry.
edges.label: First covenant blood remembered

edges.basis: Treat the later contrast as an authored comparison rather than flattening the two mountains. Hebrews places the terrifying Sinai approach beside Zion’s festal assembly without treating either location as interchangeable.
edges.label: Sinai / Zion

topic.orientation: Do not begin with a single definition and force every covenant passage into it. Follow the biblical word and its close promise-language through different people, events, signs, ceremonies, failures, renewals, prophetic hopes, meals, and later arguments. Some scenes explicitly say covenant; others are included because later Scripture itself remembers the earlier promise as covenantal.
